claims.text: The target material is a high-entropy alloy initially designed as a single-phase solid solution.
Adding a controlled amount of carbon or boron will preserve the alloy's toughness after thermal exposure and subsequent loading.
Carbon or boron interstitials induce solid-solution strengthening in the target alloy.
Carbon or boron interstitials can influence the phase stability of the target alloy.
Interstitial solid-solution strengthening can mitigate the deleterious effect of long thermal exposure on toughness.
Interstitial-induced modification of phase stability can mitigate the deleterious effect of long thermal exposure on toughness.
The interstitial-modified alloy will retain more toughness than the same alloy without added interstitials under identical exposure and loading conditions.
The applicable thermal exposure is 700 degrees Celsius for 1000 hours.
The applicable loading regimes include quasi-static loading at 10^-3 s^-1 and dynamic loading at approximately 10^3 s^-1.
A controlled carbon or boron content can be selected that does not cause significant phase segregation or precipitation.
Long exposure at 700 degrees Celsius can produce phase segregation or precipitation and degrade mechanical behavior in high-entropy alloys.
Toughness should be compared between interstitial-modified and unmodified control alloys after identical processing and loading.
Failure of the interstitial-modified alloy to show significant toughness preservation would falsify the hypothesis.

contradictions.description: The cited Ti-V-Nb-Ta evidence reports that trace oxygen and nitrogen interstitials promote phase segregation or alpha-Ti precipitation during aging and cause progressive softening, whereas the proposed mechanism treats interstitial strengthening and phase-stability modification as a route to mitigating thermal degradation. The evidence therefore supports the existence of interstitial effects but points in the opposite direction under thermal aging.
